docs.title: NeighborLend: A Hyper-Local Peer-to-Peer Rental Platform
docs.text:
Group: 3Q14, B.E. Third Year, Computer Science and Engineering Submitted to: Ms. Sandeep Kaur

Live application: https://neighborlend.vercel.app Application source code: aviraj1576/NeighborLend (linked as the code/ folder of this repository)

NeighborLend lets people rent out things they rarely use, such as tools, cameras and sports equipment, to other people nearby. It covers the whole rental: listing an item with help from an object-detection model, finding it with a location search, agreeing on a price in chat, paying the rent and a refundable deposit, recording the item's condition at handover and return, and settling damage claims.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: People often need an item for a day or two and do not want to buy it, while the same item sits unused in someone else's home nearby. Borrowing usually happens through friends or informal groups, so items are hard to find, and there is no common way to agree on a price, take a deposit, or settle a disagreement about damage.

docs.title: What the system does
docs.text:
• Accounts: registration with a CAPTCHA and email OTP verification, login, Google sign-in, profiles with a trust score.
  • Listings: item details and photos; a YOLO model trained on rentable item classes suggests what the item is from its photo; a rule-based suggestion for the daily rent and deposit.
  • Discovery: browse and search by keyword, category and distance from the user's location.
  • Chat and negotiation: a conversation per listing, with offers, counter-offers, acceptance and rejection. An accepted offer creates the booking.
  • Payment: rent and refundable security deposit through Razorpay Test Mode, with the deposit tracked in a balanced, simulated ledger.
  • Handover and return: condition photos at handover and at return, confirmed by the other party.
  • Damage claims: the lender can raise a claim, the borrower can respond, and an administrator decides any deduction. AI-based photo comparison gives advisory findings only.
  • Ratings: both parties rate each other after the rental.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The React single-page app is served from Vercel and calls a FastAPI REST API running in a Docker container on Render. Data is stored in PostgreSQL on Supabase, and listing photos in Supabase Storage. Razorpay (Test Mode) handles payments and refunds, and Brevo delivers verification emails.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Payments run in Razorpay Test Mode only, so no real money moves. The security deposit is a simulated ledger entry, not real escrow, and there are no payouts to lenders.
  • The AI damage comparison is experimental. Its results vary with lighting, angle and background, so it only advises; an administrator makes every deduction decision.
  • The object-detection model recognises only the item classes it was trained on.

docs.title: Week 3 : What Evidence a Rental Needs to Be Trusted
Goal
docs.text: Lender and borrower are usually strangers. Before designing any feature, list what can go wrong in a rental and what record would settle each case.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The rental flow from the pitch is: listing → negotiation → booking and payment → handover → rental period → return → settlement and rating.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Almost every dispute is about one question: what was the item's condition at handover, and what was it at return? A record made by only one side, or made after the dispute has started, cannot answer that question fairly.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Risk Record that settles it Made by "The item was already damaged when I got it" condition photos at handover, confirmed by the borrower lender, then borrower "The item came back damaged" return photos of the same views, reviewed by the lender borrower, then lender Disagreement about a deduction the claim, the reply and both photo sets, decided by a third party administrator Payment taken but item never handed over handover allowed only after the payment is verified system One side never reacts a deadline after which the system takes the default action system

Requirements that followed for the design:

  1. Each step is confirmed by the other party (no one confirms their own claim).
  2. Evidence is stored with the step it belongs to and cannot be replaced after that step is confirmed.
  3. A deduction from the deposit is never automatic; a person decides it.

Because

Writing the risks first gave a test for every later feature: does it create or protect one of these records? The handover state machine (Week 15) and the damage comparison (Weeks 5–8 and 16) both come from this table.

docs.title: Week 4 : The Damage Claim and Deposit Settlement Workflow for the Proposal
Goal
docs.text: Describe, for the proposal, exactly what happens to the security deposit after an item is returned, including the case where the two users disagree.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The borrower pays a refundable deposit together with the rent. After the return, the lender compares the return photos with the handover photos (Week 3).

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
There are only three outcomes, and each one must end with the whole deposit accounted for:

  1. no damage: the full deposit goes back to the borrower;
  2. damage, and the borrower accepts the claim: the agreed amount is deducted and the rest is refunded;
  3. damage, and the borrower rejects the claim: nothing can be deducted until someone independent decides.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
return photos uploaded
                     │
          lender reviews return
           │                  │
      no damage          damage claim (amount + photos)
           │                  │
   refund full deposit   borrower responds
                          │            │
                       accepts      rejects
                          │            │
              deduct agreed amount   dispute: deposit stays held
              refund the rest        until an administrator decides

Rules written into the proposal:

  • the claimed amount can never be more than the deposit;
  • if the borrower rejects the claim, the booking is marked disputed and the disputed amount stays unresolved until a platform-level decision;
  • every decision is recorded with who made it and when.

Because

Making "rejected" lead to a held deposit, rather than to either side winning, removes any reason to reject or claim falsely just to win by default. In the final system the third outcome is decided by an administrator who is neither of the two parties.

docs.title: Week 5 : Why a Simple Pixel Difference Cannot Detect Damage
Goal
docs.text: Find a way to compare a handover photo with a return photo of the same item and point out possible new damage, as an aid for the lender and the administrator.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The two photos are taken by different people, on different phones, days apart, in different places. Nothing about the camera position, the lighting or the background is controlled.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Subtracting the two images (|before − after|) marks almost everything as changed, for reasons that have nothing to do with damage:

Cause Effect on a pixel difference a slightly different angle or distance every edge moves, so every edge is "changed" different lighting or white balance the whole object changes brightness a different background large changed areas around the object glare on glossy surfaces bright patches that look like scratches blur or low resolution detail missing in one photo only

A useful comparison therefore needs, in this order: photos good enough to compare, the object separated from the background, the two views aligned geometrically, and only then a comparison that tolerates lighting changes.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
The pipeline chosen for the next weeks, built with OpenCV and NumPy:

  1. Quality gate: reject blurred, dark, over-exposed or low-resolution photos and ask for a recapture (Week 6).
  2. Alignment: match local features between the two photos and estimate a geometric transform with RANSAC (Week 7).
  3. Comparison: structural similarity (SSIM) over the aligned object area, which compares local structure rather than raw brightness (Week 7).
  4. Output: candidate regions for a person to look at, never a verdict.

Because

Each stage removes one cause of false alarms before the next stage runs. If a stage fails, the result is "inconclusive", which is honest, instead of a difference map full of false damage.

docs.title: Week 6 : A Quality Gate for Condition Photos
Problem
docs.text: A blurred or badly lit photo makes any later comparison meaningless: a blurred return photo hides scratches, and an over-exposed one looks like damage. Such photos must be caught when they are uploaded, while the user can still take another one.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Each photo arrives as an RGB image. An optional mask marks the pixels that belong to the object, so the background does not affect the measurements.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Each common problem has a simple, cheap measurement:

Problem Measurement blur, or no texture variance of the Laplacian (few strong edges → low variance) low contrast standard deviation of the grey values under- or over-exposure fraction of pixels below 10 or above 245 too small shorter side below a minimum object cut off the object mask touches the image border

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
def assess_quality(evidence_id, rgb, config, mask=None):
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(rgb, cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)
    values = gray[mask] if mask is not None and mask.any() else gray.ravel()
    laplacian = cv2.Laplacian(gray, cv2.CV_64F)
    focus = float(laplacian[mask].var() if mask is not None and mask.any() else laplacian.var())
    dark, bright = float((values < 10).mean()), float((values > 245).mean())
    reasons = []
    if min(gray.shape) < config.min_side:
        reasons.append("low_resolution")
    if focus < config.min_focus:
        reasons.append("blur_or_no_texture")
    if values.std() < config.min_contrast:
        reasons.append("low_contrast")
    if dark > config.max_clipped_fraction:
        reasons.append("underexposed")
    if bright > config.max_clipped_fraction:
        reasons.append("overexposed")
    ...

Each reason comes with a concrete instruction for the user, for example "Reduce glare and exposure; avoid direct flash on reflective surfaces" for overexposed. A photo with any reason is marked needs_recapture.

Because

The Laplacian responds to edges, so a sharp photo has many large values and a high variance, while blur spreads edges out and lowers it. Telling the user why a photo was rejected, and how to retake it, turns a rejection into a better second photo. The instruction text also warns against sharpening or upscaling a photo just to pass the check.

docs.title: Week 7 : Prototype: Aligning Two Photos and Comparing Them with SSIM
Problem
docs.text: For the prototype, compare a handover photo and a return photo of the same item and mark regions that may have changed, without marking the normal differences listed in Week 5 (angle, lighting, background).

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Both photos have passed the quality gate (Week 6), and each has a mask of the object. The two photos are never taken from exactly the same position.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Before two photos can be compared pixel by pixel, the "before" photo must be warped so that each point of the object lands where it is in the "after" photo. This needs reliable point correspondences, and a single wrong match can spoil the transform unless the estimate is robust to outliers.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Local features (SIFT) on the object only, with contrast-limited histogram equalisation (CLAHE) to reduce lighting differences, and RootSIFT normalisation of the descriptors:

detector = cv2.SIFT_create(nfeatures=1200, enable_precise_upscale=True)
gray = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8)).apply(gray)
keypoints, descriptors = detector.detectAndCompute(gray, mask.astype(np.uint8) * 255)
descriptors = np.sqrt(descriptors / np.maximum(descriptors.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True), 1e-8))

2. Mutual matching with Lowe's ratio test: a match is kept only if it passes the 0.75 ratio test in both directions (before → after and after → before).

3. RANSAC homography, with a fallback to a simpler similarity transform under the same checks. At least 12 inliers and an inlier ratio of 0.45 are required; otherwise the pair is reported as weak_geometric_support_or_view_change.

matrix, inliers = cv2.findHomography(src, dst, cv2.RANSAC, 3.0)

4. SSIM over the aligned overlap. A global gain and offset correct the overall brightness first; then a Gaussian-window SSIM map is computed, and a pixel is a change candidate only if both the SSIM difference and the absolute grey difference are large. Connected regions are kept if their area is within limits, and the 20 largest are returned:

difference = np.clip((1 - ssim_map(adjusted, gray2)) / 2, 0, 1)
proposals = (difference > config.difference_threshold) & (np.abs(adjusted - gray2) > 0.06) & overlap

A morphological closing (not an opening) joins broken pieces, because an opening would erase the one- or two-pixel-wide lines that thin scratches and cracks produce.

Because

RANSAC fits the transform to random small subsets and keeps the one most points agree with, so wrong matches do not pull it away. SSIM compares local mean, contrast and structure, so a uniform lighting change affects it far less than a scratch does. Every step can stop the pipeline with a named reason, and the output is a set of candidates for a person to review.

docs.title: Week 8 : Improvement Plan: Object Masks, an Identity Check, and Honest Results
Problem
docs.text: The prototype comparison (Week 7) assumed that both photos show the same object and that the object mask is right. With real photos, the background, hands holding the item, or a different item could produce many false candidates.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
Two small pretrained models were added in front of the geometric stage, both used only for inference (no training):

  • EfficientSAM-Ti segments the object inside a target box, giving the object mask;
  • DINOv2-S/14 turns the masked object into an embedding vector. Two photos of the same object should have similar embeddings (cosine similarity close to 1).

The pipeline is: quality gate → masks → embeddings → SIFT/RANSAC alignment → masked SSIM candidates.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: An identity check placed before alignment stops the pipeline early when the two photos may not show the same thing. A pair whose cosine similarity is below 0.65 is reported as embedding_inconsistent, and no difference map is produced for it.

docs.title: Results on Real Photos
docs.text:
Three real photo pairs were run through the full pipeline on a GPU (two drill pairs and one headphone pair):

Pair Outcome Cosine similarity drill 1 → drill 2 inconclusive 0.493 drill 1 → drill 3 inconclusive 0.462 headphones 1 → 2 inconclusive 0.453

All three stopped at the identity check, so alignment and SSIM were never reached. Looking at the masks explained part of this: one drill mask also included the fingers holding the tool, and one headphone mask contained detached pieces of background. Each run took about 13–16 seconds and around 1.5 GB of memory in the worker process.

docs.title: Conclusion for the Improvement Plan
docs.text:
• The classical pipeline is careful (it does not invent damage), but with uncontrolled photos it is mostly inconclusive.
  • Results depend strongly on how the photos are taken. Guided capture of fixed views, against a plain background, would help more than any threshold change.
  • Its run time and memory are too high for the free 512 MB server.

These findings led to the second version in Week 16: guided capture of six fixed views, and a vision-language model used as an advisory comparison.

Because

Reporting "inconclusive" with the reason is more useful than a confident wrong answer, because a deposit deduction depends on it. Lowering the 0.65 threshold until the pairs "pass" would have hidden the real problem, which was the photos and the masks.

docs.title: Week 11 : Preventing Double Booking of the Same Item
Problem
docs.text: Two borrowers negotiating for the same item at the same time could both get an accepted offer for overlapping dates. The item can only be in one place.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: An accepted offer becomes a borrow request with needed_from and needed_until dates. While the item is out, the request may also have an actual start (borrowing_started_at) and a due date (return_due_at). The check runs whenever an offer is made, countered or accepted.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Two date intervals [S1, E1] and [S2, E2] overlap exactly when S1 ≤ E2 and E1 ≥ S2. This one condition covers every case (one inside the other, partial overlap at either end, identical ranges), so no case-by-case logic is needed.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
services/negotiation.py checks both kinds of existing booking with that condition, directly in SQL:

conflict_offer = (db.query(NegotiationOffer)
    .filter(NegotiationOffer.listing_id == listing_id,
            NegotiationOffer.status == OfferStatus.accepted,
            NegotiationOffer.start_date <= end_date,
            NegotiationOffer.end_date >= start_date)
    .first())

conflict_borrow = (db.query(BorrowRequest)
    .filter(BorrowRequest.listing_id == listing_id,
            BorrowRequest.status == BorrowRequestStatus.fulfilled,
            BorrowRequest.returned_at.is_(None),
            func.coalesce(BorrowRequest.borrowing_started_at, BorrowRequest.needed_from) <= end_date,
            func.coalesce(BorrowRequest.return_due_at, BorrowRequest.needed_until) >= start_date)
    .first())

When a conflict exists, the user gets the reason with the dates, for example "Item is already booked from Nov 20, 2026 to Nov 22, 2026." The offer being countered is excluded from the check, so a counter-offer does not conflict with itself.

The rental cost uses one rule everywhere: the number of days is end − start, a same-day rental counts as one day, and an end date before the start date is rejected.

Because

coalesce uses the real dates once a rental has started and the planned ones before that, so a late return keeps blocking new bookings until the item is actually back (returned_at is set).

docs.title: Week 12 : Ratings After a Rental, and Notifications for Every Step
Goal
docs.text: After a rental, each side rates the other once. And at every step of a rental, the other party should learn that it is their turn to act.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: A rental is a BorrowRequest. The ratings are stored on it as lender_rating and borrower_rating (1–5) with an optional comment, so each rental can hold at most one rating in each direction.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A rating is only meaningful once the rental is really over. If a rating were allowed while a return was still being reviewed, it could be used as a threat during a disagreement.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Ratings. POST /{id}/rate-lender (borrower only) and POST /{id}/rate-borrower (lender only) apply three checks in order:

if current_user.id != req.borrower_id:
    raise HTTPException(403, "Only the borrower can rate the lender")
if not rating_eligible(db, req):
    raise HTTPException(409, "Ratings require confirmed return and completed financial settlement")
if req.lender_rating is not None:
    raise HTTPException(409, "Lender already rated for this rental")

rating_eligible requires a recorded return with photos, a captured payment, a completed booking and a fully settled deposit (refund processed, and refund plus deduction equal to the deposit). After saving, the rated user's aggregate rating and trust score (Week 14) are recalculated.

Notifications. One helper creates a notification with a type, a title, a message and a link to the rental:

def create_notification(db, user_id, notification_type, title, message,
                        link_url, borrow_request_id=None):
    notification = Notification(user_id=user_id, notification_type=notification_type,
                                title=title, message=message, link_url=link_url,
                                borrow_request_id=borrow_request_id)
    db.add(notification)
    return notification

The helper only adds the row; the endpoint commits it together with the action itself, for example "{name} rated you 4/5 stars for {title}." with a link to /borrow-requests/{id}.

Because

Because the notification is committed in the same transaction as the action, a user can never be told about an action that failed and was rolled back. The link takes them straight to the screen where they must act.

docs.title: Week 14 : A Trust Score that New Users Cannot Game
Problem
docs.text: A user with a single 5-star rating should not look more trustworthy than a user with forty ratings averaging 4.8. Disputes that a user lost should lower trust, and a verified email should count for something.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: For each user the database knows their ratings, the number of completed rentals, the disputes they lost, disputes settled without a clear loser ("neutral"), and whether their email is verified.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A plain average is unreliable for small counts. A Bayesian average pulls the score towards a prior until enough ratings exist: with a prior of 3.5 worth 5 ratings, one 5-star rating gives (5 + 5 × 3.5) / 6 = 3.75, not 5.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Four components, each normalised to 0–5, and a weighted total:

RATING_PRIOR = 3.5
RATING_PRIOR_COUNT = 5

def calculate_trust_components(*, ratings, transactions, losses, neutral, verified):
    rating, rating_count, average = _rating_component(ratings)   # Bayesian average, scaled to 0–5
    reliability = _clamp(5.0 * (1.0 - (losses + 0.25 * neutral) / (transactions + 5.0)))
    experience = _clamp(5.0 * (1.0 - math.exp(-transactions / 20.0)))
    verification = 5.0 if verified else 0.0
    total = round(0.45 * rating + 0.30 * reliability + 0.15 * experience + 0.10 * verification, 2)
Component Weight Behaviour rating 45 % Bayesian average of 1–5 stars reliability 30 % falls with lost disputes; a neutral one counts a quarter experience 15 % rises with completed rentals, levelling off (about 3.2 at 20 rentals) verification 10 % full marks for a verified email

The score is recalculated whenever a rating is given or a dispute is decided, and the profile page shows each component, not only the total.

Because

The "+5" in the reliability denominator works like the rating prior: one lost dispute in a user's first rental does not drop them to zero. Showing the components explains a low score instead of just displaying it.

docs.title: Week 15 : The Handover and Return Workflow as a Guarded State Machine
Problem
docs.text: After an offer is accepted, the item still has to change hands and come back. Both sides need a record of the item's condition at each step (Week 3), and neither side should be able to skip a step or act for the other.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
A rental is a BorrowRequest row. Its progress is stored in handover_status, whose allowed values come from an enum:

class HandoverStatus(str, enum.Enum):
    not_applicable = "not_applicable"
    pending = "pending"
    photos_uploaded = "photos_uploaded"                # lender uploaded item photos
    borrower_confirmed = "borrower_confirmed"          # borrower received the item
    lender_confirmed = "lender_confirmed"              # handover complete, rental active
    issue_reported = "issue_reported"
    return_photos_uploaded = "return_photos_uploaded"  # borrower uploaded return photos
    return_confirmed = "return_confirmed"              # lender approved the return
    disputed = "disputed"                              # lender disputed the return
    dispute_resolved = "dispute_resolved"              # administrator decided

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Each transition is allowed for exactly one role and only from a fixed set of previous states. If every endpoint checks both before changing anything, the whole workflow is a state machine enforced by the server, not by the user interface.

pending ─lender uploads photos→ photos_uploaded ─borrower confirms→ lender_confirmed (rental active)
        ─borrower uploads return photos→ return_photos_uploaded
        ─lender approves→ return_confirmed      or   ─lender disputes→ disputed → dispute_resolved

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Each endpoint checks the role first (HTTP 403), then the state (HTTP 409), and only then updates the row and notifies the other party:

if current_user.id != lender_id:
    raise HTTPException(403, "Only the lender can upload handover photos")
if req.handover_status not in (HandoverStatus.pending.value, HandoverStatus.photos_uploaded.value):
    raise HTTPException(409, "Handover is not in a state to upload photos")
Endpoint Who From state POST /handover/upload-photos lender pending, photos_uploaded POST /handover/borrower-confirm borrower photos_uploaded POST /handover/report-issue borrower photos_uploaded, borrower_confirmed POST /return/upload-photos borrower lender_confirmed, return_photos_uploaded POST /return/confirm lender return_photos_uploaded

Once the lender has shared the condition photos, the borrower's confirmation of receipt completes the handover and starts the rental, so the lender does not need a separate confirmation step. Handover photos can be uploaded only after the payment has been verified.

Because

403 ("not your action") and 409 ("not now") give the frontend two different errors to show. Keeping the photos on the same row as the state means the evidence for each step is stored together with the step itself. The handover tests in tests/test_handover.py exercise each guard.

docs.title: Week 16 : Damage Check, Second Version: Six Guided Views and an Advisory AI Comparison
Problem
docs.text: The classical pipeline (Weeks 5–8) was mostly inconclusive on real photos, and too heavy for the 512 MB server. The second prototype needed a damage check that works inside the real rental flow, with photos taken by ordinary users on their phones.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The damage check is a separate module, backend/damage_check/, mounted into the backend. A check belongs to one rental and collects photos in two phases, before (lender, at handover) and after (borrower, at return), each with the same six views: front, back, left, right, top and bottom.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Most failures of the first version came from the photos, not the algorithm: different sides of the object, different distances, other things in the frame. Guided capture of the same six views solves most of this before any comparison runs. Then a vision-language model can compare each before/after pair of the same view, as long as it is told clearly what does not count as damage.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Guided six-view capture in the frontend (components/damage/), with a client-side quality check before upload. By default all six views are required in both phases.

  2. One comparison per view, at most two at a time, each with a 60 s timeout and up to 4 retries on rate-limit or server errors. Photos are scaled down to at most 1024 px on the longer side before they are sent.

  3. A conservative prompt. The model is told that its main job is to avoid false alarms, and to report damage only if the defect is clearly visible in AFTER, the same spot is clearly intact in BEFORE, and it is physical damage rather than a change of light. It answers in JSON:

    {"comparable": true, "damage_detected": false, "confidence": "low",
 "findings": [], "note": "..."}

    Text inside the photos is treated as image content, never as an instruction.

  4. A cautious overall result. An error never counts as "clear":

    def aggregate_overall(results):
    for r in results:
        if r.comparable and r.damage_detected and r.confidence in ("medium", "high"):
            return "possible_damage"
    for r in results:
        if r.error or not r.comparable or r.damage_detected:
            return "needs_review"
    return "clear"

    If the AI provider cannot start (for example, no API key), the app still runs and every view becomes needs_review.

  5. People decide. The lender reviews the result and approves the return or disputes it; only an administrator can approve a deduction. If the lender does not review a return within 72 hours, it is approved automatically. This deadline is checked whenever the rental is read, with the row locked so that two requests cannot both apply it.

Because

The AI's output is advice attached to the evidence, never a decision. That matches the final report's position: the damage comparison gives moderate, inconsistent results across photographs and conditions, so it must not authorise any financial deduction on its own.

docs.title: Week 17 : Designing Test Cases for the Main Rental Workflow
Goal
docs.text: Check the main rental workflow end to end on the deployed system (neighborlend.vercel.app), not only through unit tests, and record the results in the course's test case format.

docs.title: Test Case Format
docs.text:
Each test case follows the course's Test Case Template (Doc:T_01):

  • a header: test case number and name, system, subsystem, designer, design date and a short description;
  • pre-conditions, for example "the email is not registered" and "the tester can read its inbox";
  • numbered steps, each with an action, the expected system response, and Pass/Fail and Comment columns;
  • post-conditions to check in the database afterwards, for example "the user is saved with a verified email" and "no account is created for the second email".

Every case tests the happy path and also failure conditions, such as a wrong OTP, a wrong CAPTCHA answer, a wrong password or a conflicting booking.

docs.title: Test Cases
docs.text: # Test case Subsystem Steps 1.1 Register with Email OTP Verification Authentication 7 1.2 Login and Protected Pages Authentication 5 2.1 Create Listing with AI Photo Detection Listings 8 2.2 Browse and Search Listings Listings 7 3.1 In-Chat Negotiation and Booking Conflict Negotiation 10 4.1 Handover State Machine Rental 7 4.2 Return and Dispute Rental 5

docs.title: Execution and Results
docs.text:
The cases were run on the live deployment, with Razorpay in Test Mode and a separate browser session for each user (lender and borrower). Public Mailinator inboxes were used so that the OTP emails could be read.

On the first run, four cases failed one step each:

Test case Failed step What was fixed 2.1 7 Create Listing now shows an error when a non-image file is chosen 2.2 6 Browse says when location is blocked or unavailable, and shows all listings without a distance filter 3.1 6 Accepting an offer notifies both parties and shows a success message 4.1 3 Once the lender has shared the condition photos, the borrower's receipt completes the handover and starts the rental

After the fixes were deployed, the four cases were re-run in full. All seven cases passed (49 of 49 steps).

Because

Writing the expected response before running a step is what made these failures visible. Three of the four were missing feedback to the user, which unit tests of the API would not have caught.

docs.title: Week 3 : From Use Cases to a Screen Map
Goal
docs.text: Before writing interface code, list every screen the application needs and give each one a route (URL). The frontend and the backend can then be planned around the same set of user actions.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The use cases from the pitch have four kinds of actor:

  • a guest, who can look at listings but cannot act on them;
  • a lender, who lists items and confirms handover and return;
  • a borrower, who searches, negotiates, pays and returns the item;
  • an administrator, who reviews disputes.

Lender and borrower are roles of the same registered user, not separate account types.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Many use cases act on the same object. "Send offer", "counter offer", "accept" and "reject" all belong to one conversation about one listing, so they need one screen, not four. Grouping the use cases by the object they act on (a listing, a conversation, a borrow request) gives a small set of screens.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Screen Route Use cases Login Landing / explain the service no Register, Verify email, Login /register, /verify-email, /login create account, verify OTP, log in no Browse /browse search nearby items no Listing detail /listing/:id view item, start a chat no Create listing /create-listing publish item, upload photos, AI identification, price suggestion yes My listings /my-listings edit or remove own items yes Messages /messages chat, offer, counter, accept, reject yes Borrow request /borrow-requests/:id handover, return, rating yes My borrow requests /my-borrow-requests track rentals yes Notifications /inbox read notifications yes Profile /profile, /users/:userId update profile, view trust score yes

The administrator screens (/admin/disputes) and the damage-check page were added later, once those workflows existed.

Because

One route per object keeps links shareable: a notification can point straight to /borrow-requests/<id>. Deciding early which routes need a login also fixed where the frontend has to check authentication (Week 5).

docs.title: Week 4 : Shared UI Components and Design Tokens
Goal
docs.text: Decide how every page looks, and build the small set of components that all pages use, so that screens built by different team members stay consistent.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The screen map (Week 3) contains many forms (register, create listing, offers) and many lists of cards (listings, requests, notifications). Without shared parts, each page would style its own buttons and fields.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Most visual differences between pages come from a few repeated decisions: colours, spacing, corner radius, and the states of a form field (normal, focused, error, disabled). If these are decided once, a page only has to arrange components.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Design tokens as CSS custom properties in src/design/theme.css. Pages refer to the token, never to a raw colour. The current values (after the Week 16 redesign) include:

    :root {
  --p-bg: #ffeed6;
  --p-surface: #f3e1cc;
  --p-ink: #2b061e;
  --p-muted: #76575d;
  --p-accent: #d2bf55;
  --p-border: #8e7275;
  --p-danger: #b3261e;
}

  2. Five primitives in src/components/ui/: Button, Input, Card, Modal and Badge. Input renders a text field, a <textarea> or a <select> depending on type, and always places its label and error message the same way:

    <Input id="title" label="Item name" value={title}
       onChange={(e) => setTitle(e.target.value)} error={errors.title} />

Because

Changing a token restyles every page at once, so the later redesign was mostly a matter of editing tokens and layouts, not rewriting pages. Keeping the label and the error inside Input means no form can forget to show its validation errors.

docs.title: Week 5 : One API Client and Protected Routes
Problem
docs.text: Every page calls the backend, and most calls need the user's login token. If each page builds its own request and adds the token itself, one forgotten header gives a confusing 401, and an expired token leaves the user on a page that silently fails.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The backend issues a JWT at login and expects it in an Authorization: Bearer <token> header. The frontend keeps the token in localStorage under the key nl_token.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Adding the token and reacting to an expired session are the same for every request. They belong in one place, not in every page.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. One Axios instance in src/api/client.js. A request interceptor adds the token, and a response interceptor sends the user to the login page on a 401 (except for the login and register calls themselves):

    const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: import.meta.env?.VITE_API_BASE_URL || '/api',
});

api.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = localStorage.getItem('nl_token');
  if (token) config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  return config;
});

  2. An AuthContext loads the current user once at start-up with GET /auth/me and exposes user, isAuthenticated and loading.

  3. A ProtectedRoute wrapper for every route marked "login: yes" in the screen map:

    const ProtectedRoute = ({ children }) => {
  const { isAuthenticated, loading } = useAuth();
  if (loading) return <div>Loading...</div>;
  if (!isAuthenticated) return <Navigate to="/login" />;
  return children;
};

Because

The loading check matters: without it, a logged-in user who refreshes the page is sent to /login for a moment, because the user is not known until /auth/me returns. The route guard only improves the experience; the backend still checks the token on every protected endpoint.

docs.title: Week 6 : The Create Listing Form with AI Prefill and a Price Suggestion
Goal
docs.text: Make listing an item quick: the lender uploads a photo, the category is filled in from the photo, and a daily rent and deposit are suggested. The lender can still change everything before publishing.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The backend offers two endpoints for this:

  • POST /api/ai/identify runs the item-detection model on the photo and returns predicted labels with confidences;
  • POST /api/listings/suggest-price takes the purchase price and the age of the item, and returns a daily rent and a security deposit.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Both features are only suggestions. If either endpoint is slow or fails, the lender must still be able to finish the form. A failed AI call should leave the fields empty, not block the page.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. The category is prefilled from the best prediction, and the confidence is shown as a bar so that the lender can judge it:

    <div className="confidence-track">
  <div className="confidence-bar" style={{ width: `${aiData.confidence}%` }} />
</div>
<span className="t-small muted">{aiData.confidence}% match</span>

  2. The price suggestion calls the backend. If the call fails, the page applies the same rule locally: the value falls by 15 % per year of age, the daily rent is 4 % and the deposit 20 % of that value, rounded to the nearest ₹5.

    try {
  const res = await api.post('/listings/suggest-price',
                             { purchase_price: rawPrice, age_years: rawAge });
  setSuggestion(res.data);
} catch (err) {
  const currentVal = Math.round(rawPrice * Math.pow(0.85, rawAge) * 100) / 100;
  const dailyRent = Math.round((currentVal * 0.04) / 5) * 5;
  const deposit = Math.round((currentVal * 0.20) / 5) * 5;
  setSuggestion({ current_value: currentVal, daily_rent: dailyRent,
                  security_deposit: deposit });
}

  3. The inputs are validated before the call: the purchase price must be greater than zero, and the age cannot be negative.

Because

Showing the confidence, instead of silently filling the field, keeps the lender in control of what is published. The local fallback must use exactly the same formula as the backend (services/pricing.py); otherwise the suggestion would change depending on whether the server answered.

docs.title: Week 7 : The Browse Page for the Prototype (Search, Category, Distance)
Goal
docs.text: For the prototype evaluation, show that a borrower can find items near them: search by name, filter by category, and limit the distance with a slider.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The backend search endpoint takes all filters as query parameters:

GET /api/listings/search?q=drill&category=Tools&lat=30.34&lon=76.39&radius_km=50

It computes the distance of each listing from (lat, lon) and drops those outside radius_km. A radius of 500 km or more means "no distance limit".

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The page has four inputs (text, category, radius, location) that all change the same result list. Building the query in one function, and calling it whenever any filter changes, keeps the list and the filters in sync.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
const [radius, setRadius] = useState(50);

const fetchListings = async () => {
  const params = new URLSearchParams();
  if (searchQuery) params.append('q', searchQuery);
  if (category !== 'All') params.append('category', category);
  params.append('lat', location.lat);
  params.append('lon', location.lon);
  // The last slider position (100) means "all distances".
  params.append('radius_km', radius < 100 ? radius : 9999);
  const res = await api.get(`/listings/search?${params.toString()}`);
  setListings(res.data || []);
};

useEffect(() => { fetchListings(); }, [category, radius, location]);
  • The heading says what is shown: "Listings within 50 km of …", or "all distances" at the end of the slider.
  • The location comes from the browser's geolocation API. If the user blocks it, the page falls back to an approximate location from the IP address, and then to a default hub (Patiala).
  • Each result is a ListingCard with the photo, the daily price and the distance.

Because

Sending the maximum value as "no limit" (9999 km, above the backend's 500 km cut-off) avoids a separate "all distances" flag in the API. Keeping the fallbacks explicit means the page always shows some listings, even when location access is denied. (A bug in this flow, where an older search could overwrite a newer one, was found and fixed in Week 17.)

docs.title: Week 8 : Improvement Plan: From React Native to a React + Vite Web App
Problem
docs.text: The proposal planned a mobile app in React Native with Expo. At the prototype review, the main difficulty was showing the app to others: every evaluator or tester needed the app installed on a phone, and each change had to be rebuilt for the device.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The screens built so far (Weeks 4–7) used plain React components, CSS and Axios. None of them depended on a native phone feature; the camera and location are both available to web pages through browser APIs (<input type="file" accept="image/*" capture> and navigator.geolocation).

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: For this project, a web app gives the same features with a much shorter path to users: a single URL that works on a phone or a laptop, and every push deployed automatically. The existing React code could be kept almost as it was.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Move the frontend to React + Vite. Vite serves the app in development and builds static files into dist/ for production.
  2. Use React Router for the routes from the screen map.

  3. Deploy the static build on Vercel. Because routing happens in the browser, every path must return index.html; otherwise reloading a page such as /listing/42 gives a 404 from the server. frontend/vercel.json:

    {
  "buildCommand": "npm run build:web",
  "outputDirectory": "dist",
  "rewrites": [
    { "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" }
  ]
}

  4. The backend URL comes from the environment variable VITE_API_BASE_URL, so the same build works against a local or the deployed backend.

An Android wrapper (Capacitor) was tried along the way. It was removed later because the web deployment already covered every use case.

Because

A single-page application has only one real HTML file. The rewrite rule hands every URL to that file, and React Router then decides what to show. Changing the platform at the improvement-plan stage was cheap because the UI had been built from plain React components.

docs.title: Week 11 : An SVD-Based Recommender for Listings
Goal
docs.text: Show each user a short list of listings they are likely to want, based on what users with similar activity have chatted about and borrowed.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
NeighborLend has no "like" button, so there are no explicit ratings of listings. What the database does record is implicit feedback:

  • a borrower opened a conversation about a listing;
  • a borrower sent an offer on it;
  • a booking was created for it.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The user × listing matrix built from these events is very sparse: most users have interacted with only a few of the listings. Matrix factorisation suits this case. It describes every user and every listing by a small number of latent factors, and the product of the factors gives a score even for pairs that have never interacted. Truncated SVD computes such a factorisation directly on a sparse matrix.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Build the matrix R with a weight per kind of event. A stronger signal gets a larger weight, and repeated events on the same pair add up:

    from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD

WEIGHTS = {"chat": 1.0, "offer": 2.0, "booking": 3.0}

def build_matrix(events, users, listings):
    rows = [users[u] for u, _, _ in events]
    cols = [listings[l] for _, l, _ in events]
    vals = [WEIGHTS[kind] for _, _, kind in events]
    return csr_matrix((vals, (rows, cols)), shape=(len(users), len(listings)))

  2. Factorise with k components (k is kept small because there are few users) and reconstruct the scores:

    svd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=k, random_state=0)
user_factors = svd.fit_transform(R)          # U·Σ
scores = user_factors @ svd.components_      # ≈ R, zeros filled in

  3. For a user, rank the listings by score, then remove their own listings, listings they have already booked, and listings outside their search radius. Return the top N.

  4. Cold start. A new user has an empty row, so every score is zero. For them, the recommender falls back to the most-interacted listings near their location.

Because

The reconstruction U·Σ·Vᵀ is the best rank-k approximation of R, so the filled-in values reflect patterns shared by many users rather than one user's history. The planned check is to hide one interaction per user and measure how often it appears in the top N (hit rate); as the final report notes, the relevance of the recommendations still needs a proper evaluation with more users.

docs.title: Week 12 : An SVM Intent Classifier for the Negotiation Assistant
Goal
docs.text: While negotiating in chat, a user can ask the assistant questions such as "is ₹200 a day fair for this?", "what should I counter with?" or "when do I get my deposit back?". The assistant should recognise what is being asked and answer using the real numbers of that listing and offer.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: For every conversation the backend already knows the listing's daily price, the rule-based price suggestion (Week 6), the security deposit, and the offers exchanged so far. The assistant only has to choose which answer to give and fill in these numbers.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Choosing the answer is a short-text classification problem. The messages are short and informal, and often misspelt. Word features alone miss spelling variants, while character n-grams still match them. A linear SVM on sparse TF-IDF features is a strong, fast classifier for this kind of input, and it needs relatively little training data.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Intents: price_fairness, suggest_counter, deposit_info, duration_cost, how_it_works and other.

  2. Model: word and character TF-IDF features feeding a LinearSVC:

    from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline, make_union
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC

model = make_pipeline(
    make_union(
        TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), sublinear_tf=True),
        TfidfVectorizer(analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(3, 5), sublinear_tf=True),
    ),
    LinearSVC(C=1.0),
)
model.fit(train_texts, train_intents)

  3. Low confidence: LinearSVC gives no probabilities, so the largest value of decision_function is used as the confidence. Below a threshold, the message is treated as other, and the assistant shows a short menu of the topics it can help with instead of guessing.

  4. Numbers come from rules, not from the model. For suggest_counter, the reply proposes a value between the last two offers, never below the platform minimum (MIN_DAILY_PRICE_RUPEES = 20 in constants.py). The assistant never sends an offer itself; the user still has to press "Make offer".

Because

Separating "understand the question" (the SVM) from "compute the answer" (deterministic rules) means the classifier can never invent a price. As the final report states, the assistant supports the user during negotiation but never makes the rental decision.

docs.title: Week 14 : The Chat Page: Messages and Rental Offers in One Place
Goal
docs.text: Let a borrower and a lender talk about one listing and agree on terms: make an offer, counter it, accept it or reject it, without leaving the conversation.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The backend endpoints used by the page:

Action Endpoint send a message POST /api/conversations/{id}/messages make an offer POST /api/conversations/{id}/offers counter an offer POST /api/offers/{offer_id}/counter accept / reject POST /api/offers/{offer_id}/accept, /reject

An offer contains the listing, a daily price, start and end dates, and an optional note.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: There are no WebSockets in the backend, so a new message or offer from the other user only appears when the page asks for it. Polling every few seconds works, but polling a tab that nobody is looking at wastes requests.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Visible-only polling: refresh every 5 seconds, and also immediately when the tab becomes visible or gets focus again:

    const refreshWhenVisible = () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === 'visible') fetchActiveConversation(conversationId, true);
};
const interval = window.setInterval(refreshWhenVisible, 5000);
window.addEventListener('focus', refreshWhenVisible);
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', refreshWhenVisible);

  2. One form for offer and counter. The same form is used for both; only the endpoint changes:

    if (negotiationMode === 'counter' && counterTargetOffer) {
  await api.post(`/offers/${counterTargetOffer.id}/counter`, payload);
} else {
  await api.post(`/conversations/${activeConv.id}/offers`, payload);
}

  3. Accept is confirmed and then navigates. Accepting an offer creates the borrow request, so the page asks for confirmation first, then opens the new request with a notice that the handover is pending.

  4. Server messages are shown as they are. If the backend rejects an offer (for example, the dates overlap an existing booking), its detail text is shown under the form instead of a generic error.

Because

The backend, not the page, decides whether an offer is valid. Showing its message directly means the user sees the real reason ("the item is already booked for these dates") and the frontend does not repeat the rules.

docs.title: Week 15 : Deploying the Backend on Render (Docker Build and Slow First Request)
docs.text: For the second prototype, the backend was deployed on Render as a Docker container. Two problems came up.

docs.title: Part 1 : OpenCV System Library Missing from the Docker Image
Error
docs.text: The image stopped building at the apt-get install step: the package libgl1-mesa-glx could not be installed.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The item-detection code imports OpenCV (cv2), which loads the system library libGL.so.1. The Dockerfile installs it with the other graphics libraries:

FROM python:3.11-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    libxcb1 \
    libglib2.0-0 \
    libgl1-mesa-glx \
    libsm6

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The python:3.11-slim tag is not pinned to a Debian release. It now follows Debian 13 (trixie), which no longer ships libgl1-mesa-glx. That name was only a transitional package; the library itself is in libgl1.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Install libgl1 instead of libgl1-mesa-glx.

Because

A tag such as 3.11-slim follows the latest Debian release, so package names can change under an unchanged Dockerfile. Pinning the release (for example python:3.11-slim-bookworm) makes such changes deliberate.

docs.title: Part 2 : Slow First AI Request, so Preload the Model at Startup
Problem
docs.text: The first photo upload after the server started took much longer than later ones, because the detection model was loaded inside that first request.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Loading the weights and running the first inference (which initialises the runtime) are one-off costs. They belong at application startup, not in a user's request.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Move the startup work into a FastAPI lifespan handler, and load and warm the model there with a dummy image:

# simplified from main.py
def _preload_model():
    try:
        model = YOLO(str(get_settings().ai_model_path_abs))
        model(np.zeros((640, 640, 3), dtype=np.uint8), verbose=False)  # warm-up
    except Exception as exc:
        logging.getLogger(__name__).warning(f"Model pre-load skipped: {exc}")

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    Base.metadata.create_all(bind=engine)
    os.makedirs(settings.upload_dir_abs, exist_ok=True)
    _preload_model()
    yield

app = FastAPI(title="NeighborLend API", version="1.0.0", lifespan=lifespan)

Because

A failed preload is only logged, so the API still starts if the weights are missing. The cost moves to startup, which matters less than a slow first request on a free server that sleeps when idle.

docs.title: Week 16 : Visual Redesign: an Accessibility Pass and a Blank-Page Bug
docs.text: After the second prototype, every page was moved to a common page layout and the new design tokens. Two things came out of this work.

docs.title: Part 1 : Accessibility Checklist Applied to Every Page
Problem
docs.text:
An audit of every page found the same problems repeated on many of them:

  • no <h1>, or more than one, so the page had no clear title;
  • search fields and the distance slider without a label;
  • a <button> nested inside another button or link (invalid HTML, and the inner control cannot be reached with the keyboard);
  • filter tabs that did not say which one was selected;
  • a second "skip to content" link on the listing page.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Each fix was made page by page, as a separate small commit, so that any one could be reverted alone:

{/* exactly one page title */}
<h1>…</h1>

{/* every field has a label tied to its id */}
<label htmlFor="browse-search">Search items</label>
<input id="browse-search" type="search" … />

{/* a filter button says whether it is the selected one */}
<button aria-pressed={filter === 'active'} onClick={() => setFilter('active')}>
  Active
</button>

Touch targets in the Create Listing wizard were kept at least 44 px tall on mobile.

Because

A screen reader announces the <h1> as the page title, and reads a field by its label. aria-pressed tells it which tab is active, information that otherwise exists only as a colour.

docs.title: Part 2 : Blank Pages Caused by an Undefined children in Input
Error
docs.text: After the redesign, the screens with a dropdown (Create Listing, Create Request, and the offer form in Chat) went completely blank.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The shared Input component renders a <select> when type="select" and places the caller's <option> elements inside it:

export default function Input({ id, type, label, value, onChange, error,
                                className = '', rows, ...rest }) {
  ...
  <select id={fieldId} value={value} onChange={onChange} {...rest}>
    {children}
  </select>

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: children is used but never declared: it is not in the destructured parameters, so it stays inside rest. Rendering a select throws ReferenceError: children is not defined. With no error boundary, React unmounts the whole tree and leaves an empty page.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Destructure children together with the other props:

export default function Input({ id, type, label, value, onChange, error,
                                className = '', rows, children, ...rest }) {

Because

Only the select branch reads children, so pages without a dropdown kept working. That made it look like a styling problem on some pages, not a crash in one shared component. The browser console showed the ReferenceError straight away.

docs.title: Week 17 : Two Concurrency Bugs Found on the Live Deployment
docs.text: Both bugs appeared only when several requests were in flight at once, so neither showed up when testing one action at a time on a laptop.

docs.title: Part 1 : An Older Search Response Overwrites a Newer One
Error
docs.text: On the Browse page, "all distances" sometimes showed only 5 listings after the browser blocked location access, and a keyword search sometimes showed unfiltered results.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Every filter change calls fetchListings() (Week 7), and responses can arrive in a different order than the requests were sent. A slow earlier search, such as the initial 50 km search, could finish after a newer one and replace its results.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Number each search with a counter kept in a useRef, and let only the newest one update the state:

const latestSearch = useRef(0);

const fetchListings = async () => {
  const searchId = latestSearch.current + 1;
  latestSearch.current = searchId;
  setLoading(true);
  try {
    const res = await api.get(`/listings/search?${params.toString()}`);
    if (searchId !== latestSearch.current) return;   // a newer search exists
    setListings(res.data || []);
  } catch (err) {
    if (searchId !== latestSearch.current) return;
    setListings([]);
  } finally {
    if (searchId === latestSearch.current) setLoading(false);
  }
};

Because

A useRef value survives re-renders without causing one, so every pending call compares against the same counter. An AbortController would also work and would cancel the network request as well.

docs.title: Part 2 : Damage-Check Photos Fail with HTTP 500 (Connection Pool Starvation)
Error
docs.text: The damage-check page loads several condition photos at once. Some photo requests hung for about 15 seconds and then returned HTTP 500.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The database is Supabase PostgreSQL in session-pooling mode, which allows 15 client sessions in total, so the SQLAlchemy pool had been kept very small:

return {"pool_size": 2, "max_overflow": 0, "pool_timeout": 15}

Each photo request authenticates the user through get_current_user, which uses the request's database session. The damage-check module then opens its own short session to read the photo.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Each photo request needed two connections: the request session, held until the request ended, and one more for the photo. With a pool of two and two parallel requests, each held one connection and waited for another. Neither could finish, so both waited for pool_timeout (15 s) and failed.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Return the request's connection as soon as authentication is done:

    def damage_user_id(user: User = Depends(get_current_user),
                   db: Session = Depends(get_db)) -> str:
    user_id = str(user.id)
    db.close()   # the module opens its own short sessions
    return user_id

  2. Size the pool for the real deployment. Render runs a single backend instance, so it can use more of Supabase's 15 sessions:

    return {"pool_size": 5, "max_overflow": 3, "pool_timeout": 15}

Because

A pool deadlocks when every request needs k connections at once and the pool has fewer than k × (concurrent requests). Releasing the first connection early brings k down to one at a time, and the larger pool gives headroom for several photos loading in parallel.
