docs.title: Week 3 : Choosing the Item Categories for Image-Based Identification
Goal
docs.text: Image-based identification should save the lender from typing the item type. Before collecting any data, decide which kinds of item the model must recognise first.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: NeighborLend is for items that people own but rarely use, and that a neighbour might need for a day or two: tools, sports and outdoor equipment, electronics, household appliances.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: An object detector can only recognise the classes it was trained on, and every class needs its own labelled images. Too many classes at the start means too few images per class. The first model should cover the items most likely to be listed, and leave the rest to a later, larger model.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Selection criteria for a class:

  1. it is commonly lent or rented (a drill, a ladder, a bicycle);
  2. it has a recognisable shape in an ordinary phone photo;
  3. enough example images can be collected and labelled in the time available.

The first model was planned with nine classes:

Tools Outdoor and sports Electronics Other drill, hammer, pliers, ladder bicycle, umbrella headphones, keyboard book

Rules agreed with the frontend for using the model's output:

  • the result is only a suggestion; the lender can always change it;
  • a prediction below a confidence threshold is not used at all;
  • an item outside the trained classes falls back to manual entry.

Because

A small, reliable model is more useful in the listing form than a large, unreliable one, since a wrong suggestion has to be corrected by the user. The class list was extended later (Week 16).

docs.title: Week 4 : Why YOLOv8 for Item Identification (Proposal)
Goal
docs.text: For the proposal, choose the model family for identifying an item from the lender's photo, and justify the choice.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
Requirements for the model:

  • it runs on the backend, on a CPU, for one photo at a time;
  • it answers in about a second, while the lender is filling in the form;
  • it can be trained on a small custom dataset (Week 3 classes).

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Two kinds of model could do this:

Image classifier Object detector (YOLO) output one label for the whole photo a box, a label and a confidence per object photo with background clutter the background affects the label the item is located first several items in one photo cannot report them reports each one

A detector also tells where the item is, which matters for ordinary phone photos taken on a table or the floor. YOLOv8 is a one-stage detector: it predicts boxes and classes in a single pass, which keeps inference fast.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
• Model: YOLOv8 (Ultralytics), starting from weights pretrained on the COCO dataset, then fine-tuned on our classes (transfer learning).
  • Size: the nano variant (yolov8n) first, because it is small and fast on a CPU; a larger variant only if accuracy is not enough.
  • Interface: a backend endpoint receives the photo and returns [{"label": ..., "confidence": ...}], sorted by confidence.
  • Evaluation: precision, recall, mAP@50 and mAP@50–95 on a validation set (Week 7).

Because

Transfer learning reuses the general visual features learned from COCO, so a small dataset is enough to learn the new classes. Some of our classes (bicycle, umbrella, keyboard, book) also exist in COCO, which helps the model start from useful features.

docs.title: Week 5 : Building and Labelling the Dataset in YOLO Format
Goal
docs.text: Prepare a labelled dataset for the nine classes, in the format the Ultralytics trainer expects.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
YOLO training needs, for every image, a text file with one line per object:

<class_id> <x_center> <y_center> <width> <height>

All four box values are normalised to 0–1 by the image width and height, so the labels stay valid if the image is resized.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Most labelling mistakes are silent: the trainer still runs, but learns the wrong thing. Three checks catch most of them:

  1. every image has a label file with the same name, and vice versa;
  2. every class id is between 0 and 8, and every box value is in [0, 1];
  3. near-duplicate images (the same photo resized or cropped) must not end up in both the training and the validation set, or the validation score will be too optimistic.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Folder layout and the dataset file:

dataset/
  images/train/  images/val/
  labels/train/  labels/val/

# data.yaml
path: dataset
train: images/train
val: images/val
names:
  0: bicycle
  1: book
  2: drill
  3: hammer
  4: headphones
  5: ladder
  6: keyboard
  7: pliers
  8: umbrella

A short script checks the label files before every training run:

for label in Path("dataset/labels").rglob("*.txt"):
    image = label.parent.parent.parent / "images" / label.parent.name / (label.stem + ".jpg")
    assert image.exists(), f"no image for {label}"
    for line in label.read_text().splitlines():
        cls, *box = line.split()
        assert 0 <= int(cls) <= 8, f"bad class in {label}"
        assert all(0.0 <= float(v) <= 1.0 for v in box), f"box outside image in {label}"

The split into training and validation is made per source photo, so that variants of one photo stay on the same side.

Because

The class order in data.yaml becomes part of the model: class id 2 means "drill" only because of this file. The backend must use exactly the same order when it turns predicted ids back into names (Week 17).

docs.title: Week 6 : Training the First Detection Model
Goal
docs.text: Fine-tune YOLOv8 on the nine-class dataset (Week 5) and produce a checkpoint the backend can load.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Training starts from the pretrained yolov8n.pt weights. Images are resized to 640 × 640 during training, which is also the input size used later for inference.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: With a small dataset, the model can memorise the training images (over-fitting). The validation metrics, not the training loss, show whether it is still improving. Ultralytics keeps two checkpoints: last.pt (the final epoch) and best.pt (the epoch with the best validation score), and best.pt is the one to deploy.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")                 # COCO-pretrained, transfer learning
model.train(data="data.yaml", imgsz=640)   # augmentation is on by default
metrics = model.val()                      # precision, recall, mAP on the val set

Points checked after training:

  • the class names stored in the checkpoint match data.yaml;
  • predictions on photos that were not in the dataset (taken with our own phones) look sensible;
  • the checkpoint is small enough to ship inside the backend Docker image (the trained nine-class checkpoint is under 6 MB).

The checkpoint is stored in the backend as ai_service/best_model.pt.

Because

Ultralytics applies data augmentation (mosaic, scaling, colour changes, flips) by default, which partly makes up for a small dataset. Testing on our own phone photos is closer to real use than the validation set, because lenders take photos in ordinary rooms and light.

docs.title: Week 7 : Prototype: How the Detection Model Is Evaluated
Goal
docs.text: For the prototype report, define how the detection model will be judged, and what each number means for the listing form.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
A detection counts as correct when its class is right and its box overlaps the labelled box enough. The overlap is measured by Intersection over Union:

IoU = area(predicted ∩ true) / area(predicted ∪ true)

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
The four standard metrics answer different questions:

Metric Question it answers Why it matters here Precision Of the items the model reported, how many were right? a wrong suggestion has to be corrected by the lender Recall Of the items in the photos, how many were found? a missed item only means typing it in mAP@50 Average precision over all classes, at IoU ≥ 0.5 overall detection quality mAP@50–95 The same, averaged over IoU 0.5 to 0.95 how tight the boxes are

For the listing form, precision matters more than recall: no suggestion is a small inconvenience, but a wrong suggestion can be published by mistake.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
• Evaluate on the validation split with model.val(), which reports all four metrics per class and overall.
  • Choose the confidence threshold for the app from the precision–recall trade-off, not the trainer's default: a higher threshold gives fewer but more reliable suggestions.
  • Report per-class results, because a good average can hide one class the model hardly ever gets right.

At the prototype stage, the model had been trained and checked on sample images. As written in the prototype report, the final numerical values were to be recorded after the final model evaluation.

Because

The box quality (mAP@50–95) matters less for this use than the label, because the app shows the label and not the box. Choosing the threshold by precision follows directly from how the result is used.

docs.title: Week 8 : Improvement Plan: A Rule-Based Rental Price Suggestion
Problem
docs.text: The proposal planned a regression model (scikit-learn) to suggest a rental price. When the work started, there was no dataset of rental prices for items like ours to train it on.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The lender already enters two numbers that strongly affect a fair price: the purchase price and the age of the item in years. The suggestion is only a starting point that the lender can change.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A regression model trained on a handful of made-up prices would only learn those guesses, while looking more authoritative than it is. A transparent rule, with its reasoning shown to the lender, is more honest until real rental data exists.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
backend/app/services/pricing.py:

def calculate_rental_suggestion(purchase_price: float, age_years: float) -> dict:
    """
    - Current value = purchase_price * (0.85 ** age_years)
    - Daily rent = 4% of current value, rounded to the nearest ₹5
    - Refundable security deposit = 20% of current value, rounded to the nearest ₹5
    """
    current_value = round(purchase_price * (0.85 ** age_years), 2)
    daily_rent = float(round_to_nearest_5(current_value * 0.04))
    security_deposit = float(round_to_nearest_5(current_value * 0.20))
    return {"current_value": current_value, "daily_rent": daily_rent,
            "security_deposit": security_deposit,
            "explanation": f"Estimated current value: ₹{current_value:,.2f} ..."}

Example: a drill bought for ₹5,000, two years old, has a current value of 5000 × 0.85² = ₹3,612.50, a daily rent of ₹145 and a deposit of ₹725.

Negative inputs are clamped to zero, and the response includes an explanation string that the form shows next to the numbers. The test file tests/test_suggest_price.py checks the rounding and the edge cases.

Because

The formula is easy to explain and to check by hand, and the bookings made on the platform become the data a regression model could later be trained on. The use-case and data-flow diagrams in the final report describe the suggestion as rule-based for this reason.

docs.title: Week 11 : Razorpay Test Mode: Creating an Order and Verifying the Checkout
Goal
docs.text: Let the borrower pay the rent and the refundable deposit together through Razorpay, in Test Mode only, and mark the booking as funded only when the payment is really captured.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The Razorpay flow has three steps:

  1. the backend creates an order for the exact amount;
  2. the browser opens Razorpay Checkout for that order;
  3. Checkout returns razorpay_order_id, razorpay_payment_id and razorpay_signature to the browser, which sends them to the backend.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Everything returned to the browser can be changed by the user. The backend must check the signature with its own secret, and then ask Razorpay directly for the order and the payment, before trusting either.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Order. Only the borrower can create it, only for an accepted offer, and only while the booking is awaiting_payment. The amount is the booking's own total in paise, never a value from the request.

  2. Signature. Razorpay signs order_id|payment_id with HMAC-SHA256 using the key secret:

    def verify_checkout(self, order_id, payment_id, signature):
    expected = hmac.new(self._secret.encode(),
                        f"{order_id}|{payment_id}".encode(),
                        hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return (isinstance(signature, str)
            and bool(re.fullmatch(r"[a-f0-9]{64}", signature))
            and hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature))

  3. Authoritative check. After the signature, the order and the payment are fetched from Razorpay, and every field must match the booking:

    if (order.get("id") != order_id
        or order.get("receipt") != reference
        or order.get("amount") != amount
        or order.get("currency") != "INR"
        or order.get("livemode") is True
        or payment.get("id") != payment_id):
    conflict("Authoritative provider data does not match booking")

  4. Test keys only. The provider refuses to start unless the key id matches rzp_test_…, so a live key can never be used by mistake.

All of this runs with the booking row locked (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), so two verifications of the same booking cannot run at the same time.

Because

A valid signature proves that Razorpay issued these ids, but not that they belong to this booking with this amount. Fetching the order and comparing its receipt (our own reference) and amount closes that gap.

docs.title: Week 12 : Webhooks: Verifying Them and Processing Each One Exactly Once
Problem
docs.text: If the borrower closes the browser right after paying, the verification call from Week 11 never arrives, and the booking stays unpaid although the money was taken. Razorpay solves this with webhooks: it calls our backend directly when a payment or refund changes state. But webhooks can be retried, delivered more than once, or arrive before our own API call returns.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Each webhook is a POST to /api/payments/webhook with a JSON body and two headers: X-Razorpay-Signature (HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with the webhook secret) and X-Razorpay-Event-Id.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Two properties are needed:

  1. authenticity: the signature must be checked on the raw bytes, before the JSON is parsed;
  2. idempotency: the same event id must never be applied twice, and must never be reused for a different payload.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Read the body with a size limit, then check the event id and the signature:

    raw = bytearray()
async for chunk in request.stream():
    if len(raw) + len(chunk) > WEBHOOK_MAX_BODY_BYTES:
        raise HTTPException(413, "Webhook too large")
    raw.extend(chunk)
if (not event_id or len(event_id) > 128
        or not provider.verify_webhook(bytes(raw), request.headers.get("x-razorpay-signature"))):
    raise HTTPException(400, "Invalid webhook signature or identifier")

  2. Accept only known event types (payment.captured, payment.failed, order.paid, refund.processed, refund.failed, …).

  3. Record a receipt keyed by the event id, with the SHA-256 of the body, and commit it before acting on the event:

    digest = hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()
previous = db.get(ProcessedWebhook, event_id)
if previous and previous.payload_sha256 != digest:
    raise HTTPException(409, "Webhook identifier reused with another payload")
if previous and previous.status == "processed":
    return {"received": True, "duplicate": True}

  4. Never trust amounts in the webhook. For a refund the backend does not know yet, it fetches the refund from Razorpay and uses that record.

refund.created is only recorded: a refund being created is not evidence that the money was returned.

Because

The signature is computed over the exact bytes Razorpay sent; parsing and re-serialising the JSON could change them. Storing the payload hash with the event id turns a replay into a harmless "duplicate", and a forged reuse of an old id with different contents into a 409.

docs.title: Week 14 : A Balanced, Idempotent Ledger for the Simulated Deposit
Problem
docs.text: One Razorpay Test Mode payment collects both the rent and the refundable deposit. Later the deposit is refunded in full, or partly after an approved deduction. The system must always know where every rupee is, even when a webhook or an API call is delivered twice.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
There is no real escrow account. The deposit is tracked as a simulated liability in the application's own tables (payment_models.py):

  • RentalBooking: rent and deposit for one accepted offer;
  • PaymentTransaction: payments and refunds reported by the gateway;
  • JournalTransaction and EscrowLedgerEntry: double-entry journal lines;
  • RefundIntent, RefundAttempt, RentalDispute, ProcessedWebhook, FinancialAudit.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Two classic payment bugs had to be impossible by construction:

  1. Rounding drift. Floats such as 0.1 + 0.2 cannot represent money exactly.
  2. Double posting. A retried request or a repeated webhook must not record the same money movement twice.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Money as integer paise. Amounts are converted once, with Decimal and explicit rounding, and stored as integers:

def paise(value):
    amount = Decimal(str(value))
    if not amount.is_finite() or amount < 0 or amount > Decimal("10000000"):
        raise ValueError("Invalid currency value")
    return int((amount * 100).quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))

Every journal must balance. Lines are (account, side, amount), and total debits must equal total credits. When a payment is captured:

post(db, booking, "funding:" + booking.id, [
    ("gateway_clearing",    "DEBIT",  booking.total_amount_paise),
    ("rental_fee_clearing", "CREDIT", booking.rental_fee_paise),
    ("escrow_deposit_held", "CREDIT", booking.security_deposit_paise),
], "TEST MODE: payment funding; simulated accounting")

The database enforces the same rule with a check constraint: CHECK (debit_paise = credit_paise AND debit_paise > 0).

Idempotency through a reference. Each posting has a unique reference ("funding:<booking>", "settlement:<booking>"). If it has already been posted, post() returns the existing journal, but only if the stored lines are identical; otherwise it raises an error instead of silently recording a different movement under the same reference:

# simplified from escrow_service.post()
existing = db.scalar(select(JournalTransaction)
                     .where(JournalTransaction.reference == reference))
if existing:
    if (existing.booking_id != booking.id or existing.debit_paise != total
            or sorted(stored_lines) != sorted(lines)):
        raise ValueError("Journal idempotency reference conflicts with its immutable posting")
    return existing

Because

The journal is append-only: corrections are new balanced postings, never edits. The balance of any account can be recomputed from the journal lines, and a retried operation is harmless.

docs.title: Week 15 : Refunds: Authorising a Settlement Before Any Money Moves
Problem
docs.text: At the end of a rental the deposit goes back to the borrower, in full or minus an approved deduction. A refund is the one operation that sends money out, so a bug or a double click must never refund the wrong amount, refund twice, or deduct money that nobody approved.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The ledger (Week 14) records where the deposit is. A refund is made through Razorpay Test Mode against the original payment. Deductions come from a damage claim, which the two users may dispute.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: "Deciding how much to refund" and "sending the refund" are two different steps, done by different people, at different times. Keeping them apart, with a stored record between them, makes each one checkable on its own.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. A settlement intent records the decision. There is at most one per booking, the deduction must be a whole number of paise between zero and the deposit, and repeating the same decision returns the existing intent:

    existing = db.scalar(select(RefundIntent).where(RefundIntent.booking_id == booking.id))
if existing:
    if existing.kind != kind or existing.deduction_paise != deduction:
        conflict("Settlement is already authorized with different terms")
    return existing
if (booking.payment_status != "captured" or type(deduction) is not int
        or not 0 <= deduction <= booking.security_deposit_paise):
    conflict("Invalid settlement allocation")
amount = booking.security_deposit_paise - deduction

  2. Deductions in a dispute need an independent administrator, a written reason, and recorded return evidence:

    if not admin or actor in {booking.borrower_id, booking.lender_id}:
    raise HTTPException(403, "An independent human administrator must review deductions")
if not reason.strip():
    raise HTTPException(422, "Administrator resolution requires a reason")

  3. Executing the refund recomputes the expected amount from the booking and refuses to continue if the stored intent does not match it ("Refund allocation integrity failed"). A refund already dispatching must be reconciled with Razorpay before a retry.

  4. An allow-list of gateway operations. The Razorpay adapter can only create orders, read orders, payments and refunds, and create a normal refund. Any other path is rejected even when called from Python code:

    # This adapter has no capture, payout, transfer, account or settlement
# endpoint. Reject unsupported paths even when called from Python code.
raise ProviderError("unsupported_provider_operation")

Every step runs with the booking row locked and writes a FinancialAudit record with the actor.

Because

The intent is the single source of truth for the amount: the execution step does not take an amount from anyone, it only checks and carries out the recorded decision. As the final report states, AI damage results are only advice; a deduction always needs a person who is not one of the two parties.

docs.title: Week 16 : A Larger Model, and Uploads That Were Not Using It
Part 1 : Extending the Classes with a YOLOE Model
docs.text:
The nine-class model (Week 6) missed many items that people actually listed. A new checkpoint, neighborlend_yoloe_best.pt, was trained on 24 classes:

Group Classes Tools electric_drill, screwdriver, wrench, hammer Electronics smartphone, laptop, camera, headphones, keyboard, drone Outdoor and sports bicycle, scooter, tent, umbrella, basketball, dumbbell, barbell, camping_chair Home microwave, kettle, blender Travel and music backpack, suitcase, guitar

dumbbell is excluded from the predictions shown in the app (EXCLUDED_CLASSES), so 23 classes are used. A CLASS_MAP turns model names into display names, for example electric_drill → "Drill".

docs.title: Part 2 : Uploads Were Not Using the New Model
Problem
docs.text: After the new checkpoint was added, photo uploads during listing creation still did not identify items with it.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The backend had two separate model loaders:

  • services/ai_identifier.py, used by /api/ai/identify, loaded the YOLOE checkpoint and limited predictions to the allowed classes;
  • services/ml_service.py, used by the upload route, had its own loader with the plain YOLO class, and read the model path from the settings, whose default still pointed at the old file:
# config.py
ai_model_path: str = "./ai_service/best_model.pt"
ai_confidence_threshold: float = 0.45

The startup preload also warmed this second loader, not the one used by /api/ai/identify.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Two code paths that should behave the same each had their own copy of the model-loading logic, and only one copy had been updated. Testing /api/ai/identify looked correct, while users going through the upload flow got the old behaviour.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Keep one loader. ml_service now delegates to ai_identifier:

from app.services.ai_identifier import identify_item

def detect_objects(image_bytes: bytes):
    return [{"class": p["label"], "confidence": round(p["confidence"], 4)}
            for p in identify_item(image_bytes)["predictions"]]

The default settings point at the trained checkpoint, with a threshold suited to it:

ai_model_path: str = "./ai_service/models/neighborlend_yoloe_best.pt"
ai_confidence_threshold: float = 0.25

The same path change was made in .env.example, compose.yaml and render.yaml. The tests in tests/test_ai_model_connectivity.py check that uploads use the same class ids and filtering as identification, that startup warms the shared instance, and that uploads still work when the model is missing.

Because

Duplicated set-up code drifts apart. With one function owning the model, the next model change has to be made in one place only.

docs.title: Week 17 : Running the Detector with ONNX Runtime on a Small Server
Problem
docs.text: The deployed backend has 512 MB of memory and no GPU. Loading PyTorch and Ultralytics only to run one model left too little memory for the rest of the application (see Vansh's Week 17 entry).

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
A YOLO model can be exported to ONNX, a portable model format, and run with ONNX Runtime, which is much smaller than PyTorch. The backend exports the checkpoint once if no .onnx file exists:

loaded.export(format="onnx", imgsz=640, dynamic=False, simplify=False)

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Without Ultralytics, the work it normally does around the model has to be written by hand, and it must match the training exactly:

  1. pre-processing: resize with the same letterbox padding used in training;
  2. decoding: the raw output is a (1, 4 + C, 8400) tensor, i.e. 8400 candidate boxes, each with a box (cx, cy, w, h) and one score per class;
  3. non-maximum suppression (NMS): remove overlapping boxes for the same object.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Letterbox to 640 × 640, keeping the aspect ratio and padding with grey (114), then scale to 0–1 and reorder to channels-first:

scale = 640 / max(w, h)
nw, nh = int(w * scale), int(h * scale)
img_resized = img.resize((nw, nh), Image.Resampling.BILINEAR)
new_img = Image.new("RGB", (640, 640), (114, 114, 114))
new_img.paste(img_resized, ((640 - nw) // 2, (640 - nh) // 2))
arr = np.array(new_img, dtype=np.float32).transpose(2, 0, 1)[None] / 255.0

Decode by taking the best class per box and dropping boxes below the confidence threshold (0.25). The number of class columns tells which class list applies: 9 for the first model, 24 for the YOLOE model.

out = session.run(None, {input_name: arr})[0][0].T     # (8400, 4 + C)
boxes, scores = out[:, :4], out[:, 4:]
class_name_dict = NINE_CLASS_NAMES if scores.shape[1] == 9 else YOLOE_NAMES
max_scores, best_classes = scores.max(axis=1), scores.argmax(axis=1)
mask = max_scores >= conf_thresh

NMS in NumPy (IoU threshold 0.45): keep the highest-scoring box, drop the boxes that overlap it by more than the threshold, and repeat. Predictions of excluded classes are removed, names are mapped to display names, and the result is sorted by confidence.

Because

The model only gives correct results on inputs prepared exactly like its training images, so the letterbox size and padding must match the export (640, grey 114). The ONNX session is created once and reused, and a smaller 12 MB ONNX model is the one served in production (the YOLOE export is about 99 MB), which keeps memory inside the server's limit.

docs.title: Week 3 : Listing the API Resources and Agreeing on Conventions
Goal
docs.text: Turn the use cases into a list of REST resources, so that the frontend and the backend can be developed in parallel against the same contract.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The backend is written in Python with FastAPI, which generates interactive OpenAPI (Swagger) documentation at /docs from the route definitions. The frontend team (Week 3 screen map) needed to know which calls each screen would make.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Most use cases are either create/read a thing (a listing, a message) or move a thing to its next state (accept an offer, confirm a return). The first kind maps to plain resources; the second is clearer as a named action under the resource than as a generic PATCH of a status field.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Area Prefix Examples Accounts /api/auth POST /register, POST /verify-email, POST /login, GET /me Listings /api/listings POST /, GET /search, GET /{id}, PUT /{id} Chat and offers /api POST /conversations/{id}/messages, POST /offers/{id}/accept Rentals /api/borrow-requests POST /{id}/handover/..., POST /{id}/return/... Notifications /api/notifications GET /

Conventions agreed for every router:

  • plural nouns for collections; actions as sub-paths (/offers/{id}/counter);
  • 401 not logged in, 403 logged in but not allowed, 404 not found, 409 not allowed in the current state, 422 invalid input;
  • errors return {"detail": "<message for the user>"}, so the frontend can show the text directly.

Each area is a separate APIRouter registered in main.py with its prefix and a tag, so Swagger groups the endpoints by area.

Because

Separating 403 from 409 tells the frontend whether to hide an action (the user may never do it) or only disable it for now (wrong state). Agreeing on the error shape once meant no screen needed special error handling.

docs.title: Week 4 : The Data Model for the Proposal
Goal
docs.text: Define the main tables and their relationships for the proposal, so that the rental can be traced from listing to return and settlement.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The proposal names eight entities: User, Item, Booking, Offer, Payment, Evidence, Dispute and Review. The backend uses SQLAlchemy models with UUID primary keys.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Some of the proposed entities are better modelled as roles or columns than as separate tables:

  • borrower and lender are both User rows; the role depends on the rental;
  • an "Item" exists only as a listing, so Listing is the item;
  • a review is one rating in each direction per rental, so it fits as columns on the rental instead of a separate table.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Table Purpose Key relations users account, verification flag, trust score listings the item, price per day, deposit, location, AI label owner_id → users listing_photos photo URLs, one marked as cover listing_id → listings conversations one chat per borrower, lender and listing listing_id → listings messages chat messages, including system messages conversation_id negotiation_offers offer and counter-offer terms conversation_id borrow_requests the rental: status, handover state, photos, ratings listing_id, borrower_id notifications messages to a user, with a link user_id

Money fields in the later payment tables are stored as integer paise (BigInteger), never as floating point.

Because

Fewer tables means fewer joins in every rental screen, and the class diagram in the final report keeps the same scope note: no separate Item, Category or Escrow table, and AI labels stored on the listing.

docs.title: Week 5 : Backend Skeleton: Settings, Database Sessions and Routers
Goal
docs.text: Set up the FastAPI project so that every later feature follows the same pattern for configuration, database access and routing.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The same code has to run in three places: on a laptop with SQLite, in Docker with PostgreSQL, and in the tests. Only the configuration differs.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: If configuration is read in many places with os.environ, a missing value is found only when that code path runs. Reading it once into a typed object fails at startup instead, with the name of the missing setting.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Typed settings with pydantic-settings, read from the environment or a .env file, and created once:

    class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str = "sqlite:///./neighborlend.db"
    jwt_secret: SecretStr = Field(repr=False, frozen=True)
    jwt_algorithm: Literal["HS256"] = Field(default="HS256", frozen=True)
    jwt_expire_minutes: int = 60 * 24 * 7
    ...

@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()

    SecretStr keeps secrets out of logs and error messages.

  2. One database session per request, opened and always closed by a dependency:

    def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()

    SQLite needs check_same_thread=False, because FastAPI may use the session from a different thread than the one that created it.

  3. One router per area, registered with a prefix and a tag:

    app.include_router(auth.router, prefix="/api/auth", tags=["Auth"])
app.include_router(listings.router, prefix="/api/listings", tags=["Listings"])

Because

With Depends(get_db), a test can replace the database for the whole app in one line, and the finally block guarantees that connections go back to the pool even when an endpoint raises an exception.

docs.title: Week 6 : Password Hashing and JWT Authentication
Goal
docs.text: Let users register and log in, and let every protected endpoint know who is calling, without storing passwords in a readable form.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The frontend stores a token after login and sends it as Authorization: Bearer <token> (Aviraj's Week 5 entry). The backend has no server-side session store.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Two separate problems need two separate tools:

  • storing passwords: a slow, salted hash, so that a leaked database does not reveal passwords; bcrypt adds a random salt to every hash;
  • identifying the caller: a signed token that the server can check without a database lookup of a session; a JWT signed with a secret key does this.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    return bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode("utf-8"), bcrypt.gensalt()).decode("utf-8")

def verify_password(plain: str, hashed: str) -> bool:
    return bcrypt.checkpw(plain.encode("utf-8"), hashed.encode("utf-8"))

def create_access_token(user_id: str) -> str:
    expire = datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(minutes=settings.jwt_expire_minutes)
    return jwt.encode({"sub": user_id, "exp": expire},
                      settings.jwt_secret.get_secret_value(),
                      algorithm=settings.jwt_algorithm)

A dependency turns the token into a user, and rejects unverified accounts:

def get_current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme),
                     db: Session = Depends(get_db)) -> User:
    user_id = decode_access_token(token)
    if user_id is None:
        raise credentials_exception          # 401
    user = db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()
    if user is None or not user.is_verified:
        raise credentials_exception
    return user

Any endpoint that needs a logged-in user declares current_user: User = Depends(get_current_user).

Because

The exp claim makes a stolen token useless after it expires, and the signature makes it impossible to change the sub (user id) without the secret. Checking is_verified inside the dependency means no endpoint can forget that unverified accounts must not act.

docs.title: Week 7 : The Listings API for the Prototype
Goal
docs.text: For the prototype, connect the Create Listing and Browse screens to real endpoints: create a listing with photos, edit it, and keep other users from changing it.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: A listing has a name, category, description, daily price, deposit, location, an optional AI label with its confidence, and one or more photo URLs. Its status is one of draft, published, paused or removed.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Three rules must hold no matter what the frontend sends:

  1. the owner is the logged-in user, never a value from the request body;
  2. only the owner can edit a listing;
  3. a listing that is currently being rented must not change its terms.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Create. The owner comes from the token, and the first photo becomes the cover:

listing = Listing(owner_id=current_user.id, name=data.name, ...,
                  status=ListingStatus.published if data.publish else ListingStatus.draft)
db.add(listing)
db.flush()                                   # assigns listing.id
for i, url in enumerate(data.photo_urls):
    db.add(ListingPhoto(listing_id=listing.id, url=url, is_cover=(i == 0)))
db.commit()

Update. The owner check is part of the query, and status changes follow an explicit table:

listing = (db.query(Listing)
             .filter(Listing.id == listing_id, Listing.owner_id == current_user.id)
             .with_for_update().first())
if not listing:
    raise HTTPException(404, "Listing not found or unauthorized")
if has_content_changes and _listing_is_in_use(db, listing.id):
    raise HTTPException(409, "This listing cannot be edited while it is being rented.")

allowed_transitions = {
    ListingStatus.draft: {ListingStatus.published},
    ListingStatus.published: {ListingStatus.paused},
    ListingStatus.paused: {ListingStatus.published},
}

Because

Filtering by owner_id in the query answers "not found" for someone else's listing, which does not reveal whether it exists. with_for_update() locks the row, so two simultaneous edits cannot both pass the "in use" check. The explicit transition table makes an invalid status change (for example, removed back to published) a clear 409 instead of a silent update.

docs.title: Week 8 : Improvement Plan: Nearby Search with the Haversine Formula
Problem
docs.text: The proposal planned PostgreSQL with the PostGIS extension for location-based search. For the improvement plan, the search had to work on every database the project uses, including SQLite for local development and tests, where PostGIS is not available.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Each listing stores latitude and longitude as plain numbers. The search endpoint receives the user's position and a radius: GET /api/listings/search?lat=..&lon=..&radius_km=...

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: At the scale of a student project (hundreds of listings, not millions), computing the distance to each published listing in Python is fast enough, and it needs no database extension. The great-circle distance between two points on a sphere is given by the haversine formula.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
def haversine(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    R = 6371  # Earth radius in km
    dlat = math.radians(lat2 - lat1)
    dlon = math.radians(lon2 - lon1)
    a = (math.sin(dlat / 2) ** 2
         + math.cos(math.radians(lat1)) * math.cos(math.radians(lat2))
         * math.sin(dlon / 2) ** 2)
    return R * 2 * math.asin(math.sqrt(a))

The search first filters in SQL (published, category, name ILIKE), then computes distances, keeps those inside the radius, and sorts by distance. A radius of 500 km or more means "no limit"; listings without coordinates are then shown at the end.

If the browser does not share a location, GET /api/listings/detect-location estimates it from the client's IP address (reading the first address in X-Forwarded-For behind Render's proxy), and falls back to a default hub, Patiala (30.3362, 76.3922).

Because

Filtering in SQL first keeps the Python loop short. PostGIS remains the path for growth: a spatial index would avoid computing the distance to every listing once there are many of them.

docs.title: Week 11 : Registration with a CAPTCHA and an Email OTP
Goal
docs.text: Stop automated sign-ups, and make sure every account belongs to a real email address before the user can list or borrow anything.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Registration is POST /api/auth/register, then POST /api/auth/verify-email with a 6-digit code sent by email. get_current_user already rejects unverified accounts (Week 6).

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Both the CAPTCHA and the OTP are short secrets that an attacker could try to guess or reuse. Each one therefore needs an expiry, a limit on attempts, and storage that does not reveal the value.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Math CAPTCHA. The server creates the question and stores only the answer, with a 5-minute expiry. A challenge can be checked only once: the row is locked, compared, and deleted whether the answer was right or wrong.

num1, num2 = random.randint(1, 10), random.randint(1, 10)
question = f"{num1} + {num2} = ?"
...
challenge = db.query(CaptchaChallenge).filter(...).with_for_update().first()
is_valid = challenge.expires_at > datetime.utcnow() and int(answer) == challenge.answer
db.delete(challenge)
db.commit()

Email OTP. The code comes from the secrets module and is stored only as an HMAC, keyed with the server secret:

def create_email_otp() -> str:
    return f"{secrets.randbelow(1_000_000):06d}"

def hash_email_otp(user_id: str, code: str) -> str:
    message = f"{user_id}:{code}".encode("utf-8")
    return hmac.new(settings.jwt_secret.get_secret_value().encode("utf-8"),
                    message, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

def verify_email_otp(user_id, code, expected_hash) -> bool:
    return hmac.compare_digest(hash_email_otp(user_id, code), expected_hash)

A code expires after 10 minutes. After 5 wrong attempts the endpoint answers 429 Too many incorrect codes and the user must request a new code.

Because

There are only one million 6-digit codes, so a plain hash could be reversed by trying them all; an HMAC needs the server's secret as well. Including the user id in the message means a code is valid only for that user. compare_digest takes the same time whether the first or the last character differs, so response times reveal nothing about the code.

docs.title: Week 12 : Moving the Database to Supabase PostgreSQL
Problem
docs.text: Until now the backend used a local SQLite file. A deployed backend needs a database that survives container restarts and can be reached from Render. Supabase provides a hosted PostgreSQL database (and file storage) on a free plan.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Supabase is reached through its connection pooler. In session mode it allows 15 client sessions in total, shared by every process that connects. The pooler also closes connections that stay idle for a while.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Three things change when moving from a local file to a shared, hosted database:

  1. the number of connections is a shared, limited resource;
  2. a pooled connection may already be closed when the app tries to use it;
  3. creating or altering tables on startup now changes a shared production database, so it must not happen automatically.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. A small connection pool for PostgreSQL URLs (SQLite gets no pool options):

    def _pool_options_for_url(database_url):
    if not database_url.startswith("postgresql"):
        return {}
    return {"pool_size": 2, "max_overflow": 0, "pool_timeout": 15}

    (Raised to 5 + 3 in Week 17 after a starvation bug; see Aviraj's journal.)

  2. pool_pre_ping=True, so SQLAlchemy tests each connection with a cheap query before handing it out and replaces it if the pooler has closed it.

  3. No automatic DDL on hosted Supabase. Schema creation runs only when AUTO_MIGRATE is set, and even then it refuses a Supabase host:

    def require_generic_schema_target_allowed(target_engine):
    """Hosted Supabase DDL must use separately reviewed SQL, never initialization."""
    ...
    if hostname.endswith((".supabase.co", ".supabase.com")):
        raise RuntimeError("Generic schema initialization is disabled for hosted Supabase.")

    Schema changes for Supabase are written as reviewed SQL files under backend/supabase/migrations/ and applied by hand.

Because

create_all and ad-hoc ALTER TABLE calls are convenient on a laptop, but on a shared database a mistake cannot be undone by deleting a file. Making the guard check the host name means the protection does not depend on someone remembering to set an environment variable.

docs.title: Week 14 : One Container Setup for Local Development and Render
Goal
docs.text: Let every team member start the full stack with one command, and deploy the same backend image to Render without copying secrets into the repository.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The backend is built from backend/Dockerfile; the frontend has its own frontend/Dockerfile. Render can deploy a Docker service described by a render.yaml blueprint.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Two failures were common when someone set up the project:

  • a missing environment variable was discovered only when a request failed;
  • the frontend started before the backend could reach the database, so the first page showed connection errors.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
compose.yaml runs the backend and the frontend. Required variables use the ${VAR:?message} form, so Compose refuses to start and prints what is missing:

backend:
  environment:
    DATABASE_URL: ${DATABASE_URL:?Set DATABASE_URL to the PostgreSQL connection string in the project .env file}
    JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET:?Set JWT_SECRET in the project .env file}
  healthcheck:
    test: [CMD, python, -c, "from urllib.request import urlopen; urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/health', timeout=5)"]
    interval: 30s
    start_period: 60s
frontend:
  depends_on:
    backend:
      condition: service_healthy

The health endpoint checks the database, not just the process:

@app.get("/api/health")
def health():
    with engine.connect() as connection:
        connection.execute(text("SELECT 1"))
    return {"status": "ok"}

render.yaml deploys the same Dockerfile with healthCheckPath: /api/health. Every secret (database URL, JWT secret, Supabase key, email key) is declared with sync: false, which means its value is entered once in the Render dashboard and never committed. Safe defaults are fixed in the file, for example APP_ENV: production, AUTO_MIGRATE: "false" and PAYMENT_PROVIDER: disabled.

Because

A health check that runs SELECT 1 makes "healthy" mean "able to serve requests". Failing fast on a missing variable turns a confusing runtime error into a one-line message at startup.

docs.title: Week 15 : Listing Photos Lost on Redeploy, so Move Them to Supabase Storage
Problem
docs.text:
Listing photos did not display reliably on the deployed site. Photos saved in the backend's local uploads/ folder disappear whenever Render rebuilds or restarts the container, and the backend already warned about this at startup:

Supabase Storage is not configured; production uploads will use ephemeral local storage.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
services/storage_service.py uploads listing photos to a Supabase Storage bucket. At runtime it tried to create the bucket, and if that failed, to update it to public:

try:
    supabase.storage.create_bucket(bucket_name, options={"public": True})
except Exception:
    try:
        supabase.storage.update_bucket(bucket_name, options={"public": True})
    except Exception as exc:
        raise HTTPException(500, f"Could not configure Supabase bucket '{bucket_name}': {exc}")

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Creating or reconfiguring a bucket is an infrastructure change and should not happen inside a user's upload request. When it failed, the user saw a generic 500 error that did not say what was wrong.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Use one fixed bucket, listing_photos, and only check it. If it is missing or private, fail with a clear 503 message:

    bucket = supabase.storage.get_bucket(bucket_name)
is_public = bucket.get("public") if isinstance(bucket, dict) else getattr(bucket, "public", None)
if is_public is not True:
    raise HTTPException(503,
        f"Make the existing Supabase Storage bucket '{bucket_name}' public to display listing photos.")

  2. In production, create_listing accepts only photo URLs from this bucket (HTTP 422 otherwise); local /uploads/ URLs are allowed only in development.

  3. Add backend/scripts/migrate_listing_photos_to_supabase.py to copy older /uploads photos into the bucket and update their database rows. It runs as a read-only dry run unless --apply is passed, and production also needs --confirm-production-write.

Because

The bucket is now set up once, by a person, in the Supabase dashboard; the application only checks that setup and reports exactly what to fix. Making the migration script a dry run by default means running it by mistake changes nothing.

docs.title: Week 16 : Integrating the Payment Module and Fixing CORS for Vercel
Part 1 : Merging the Payment Subsystem into the Main Branch
Problem
docs.text: The payment and deposit subsystem (Tikshan's journal) was built on its own branch, integration/payment-main. The hardest part of merging it into main was one file, pages/BorrowRequestDetail.jsx, which by then rendered every stage of a rental: handover photos, receipt, return, inspection, payment and dispute.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Both branches needed to change this page, each for different stages, but in the same long file. As long as one page owns every stage, every change to any stage touches it.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
The page was split into one component per stage, and the page now only decides which one to show:

Component Stage PaymentCheckout, PaymentBreakdown, PaymentStatus paying rent and deposit HandoverConfirmation borrower confirms receipt ReturnSubmission borrower uploads return photos ReturnInspection lender reviews the return EscrowStatusCard, DepositRefundStatus where the deposit is DisputeSection claims and responses

This made BorrowRequestDetail.jsx several hundred lines shorter, and components/payments.test.js was added to test the payment display logic.

Because

Small components with one job each can be changed in parallel without conflicts, and each can be tested on its own.

docs.title: Part 2 : Requests from Vercel Blocked by CORS
Error
docs.text: The frontend on Vercel preview deployments could not call the backend. The browser reported a CORS error, and the backend logs showed no failing request.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The allowed origins were a fixed list (CORS_ORIGINS). Every Vercel preview deployment gets its own sub-domain of vercel.app, so the list could never contain all of them.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Allow a pattern as well as the fixed list: localhost on any port for development, and any sub-domain of vercel.app:

    allow_origin_regex=r"^https?://(localhost|127\.0\.0\.1)(:\d+)?$|^https://([a-zA-Z0-9_-]+\.)?vercel\.app$"

  2. Wrap the whole application in CORSMiddleware, not only the FastAPI app's middleware stack:

    _fastapi_app = app
app = CORSMiddleware(_fastapi_app, allow_origins=settings.cors_origin_list,
                     allow_origin_regex=..., allow_credentials=True,
                     allow_methods=["*"], allow_headers=["*"])
app.dependency_overrides = _fastapi_app.dependency_overrides

Because

An unhandled exception produces a 500 response outside the normal middleware stack, without CORS headers. The browser then reports a CORS error and hides the real 500, which is what made this hard to diagnose. With the outer wrapper, errors also carry the headers and appear in the console as what they are. The last line keeps the tests' dependency overrides working through the wrapper.

docs.title: Week 17 : Two Problems that Appeared Only in Production
Part 1 : Verification Emails Not Delivered from Render
Error
docs.text: Registration sends a 6-digit OTP by email (Week 11). It worked locally, but on the deployed backend the email never arrived: sending timed out.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: services/email.py sent the OTP through Brevo's SMTP relay with smtplib, on port 587 (STARTTLS).

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Cloud hosts such as Render block outbound connections on the SMTP ports 25, 465 and 587 to prevent spam. The code was correct; the network path was closed. HTTPS on port 443 is not blocked, and Brevo offers a REST API for transactional email.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Send through Brevo's HTTPS API first, and keep SMTP as a fallback:

def _send_via_brevo_api(recipient: str, code: str, settings) -> bool:
    payload = {
        "sender": {"name": "NeighborLend", "email": settings.smtp_from_email},
        "to": [{"email": recipient}],
        "subject": "Your NeighborLend verification code",
        "textContent": f"Your NeighborLend verification code is {code}. ...",
    }
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        "https://api.brevo.com/v3/smtp/email",
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8"), method="POST",
        headers={"api-key": api_key, "Content-Type": "application/json"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) as resp:
        return resp.status in (200, 201, 202)

The function returns False instead of raising on HTTP errors and timeouts, so the caller can fall back to SMTP. Tests in tests/test_email_service.py cover these paths. Registration also stays usable when no email channel works.

Because

When a feature works locally but times out in the cloud, check the network path before the code. Using the standard library's urllib avoided adding a dependency to the Docker image.

docs.title: Part 2 : Keeping AI Inference Inside Render's Memory Limit
Problem
docs.text: The backend runs on Render's free instance with 512 MB of memory. Loading PyTorch together with the detection model used most of it, and photo uploads that ran item identification were failing on the deployed backend.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: services/ai_identifier.py imported PyTorch and Ultralytics at import time, so every process paid for them even though production only runs the ONNX model through ONNX Runtime (Tikshan's Week 17 entry).

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
PyTorch is needed only for a fallback path, so importing it at startup wasted memory. Two more details mattered:

  • ONNX Runtime's CPU memory arena keeps freed buffers for reuse, which raises peak memory;
  • a call to glibc's malloc_trim through ctypes, meant to return memory to the OS, was itself causing crashes.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Lazy imports: only check that Ultralytics is installed; import torch and the model class inside _get_model() when the fallback is used:

    YOLO_AVAILABLE = importlib.util.find_spec("ultralytics") is not None

  2. No PyTorch fallback in production: without an ONNX session, return "model unavailable" instead of loading the large PyTorch model.

  3. A smaller ONNX footprint:

    opts = ort.SessionOptions()
opts.enable_cpu_mem_arena = False
opts.intra_op_num_threads = 1
opts.inter_op_num_threads = 1

  4. No native calls: remove malloc_trim, and replace OpenCV's NMSBoxes with a short NumPy implementation of non-maximum suppression.

/api/ai/status now reports the process's resident memory (memory_rss_mb). After these changes, peak memory stayed at about 238 MB.

Because

In a memory-limited container, what is imported matters as much as what is used. Reporting memory through a status endpoint makes the next problem of this kind a measurement rather than a guess.
